traditions.name: Tequila
traditions.origin: Born in and around the town of Tequila, Jalisco; the modern industry grew from valley and highland haciendas.
traditions.history: One of México's oldest regulated spirits; the denomination of origin is limited to designated municipalities, mainly in Jalisco.
traditions.legalStatus: Spirit with its own Denomination of Origin; NOM-006-SCFI-2012 defines the legal classes blanco (which may receive brief permitted maturation up to the reposado window), joven or oro, reposado, añejo and extra añejo, each with oak-resting minimums. Tequila also comes in two composition categories — 100% de agave and tequila (mixed agave and other sugars) — which are composition facts, not quality grades. Cristalino is a finishing/marketing style, not a legal class.
traditions.materials: Blue weber agave (Agave tequilana), cultivated; 100% de agave tequila uses only agave sugars, while the other legal composition category permits other sugars alongside agave — a disclosed composition fact, not a quality grade.
traditions.practices: Steam cooking in hornos or autoclaves, tahona or roller-mill extraction, fermentation, double distillation, optional oak resting.
traditions.diversity: Valley agave tends to taste savoury and vegetal, highland agave sweeter and floral; class terms are spirit-specific.
traditions.sustainability: Agave tequilana is cultivated at scale, so tequila does not share the wild-population pressure of wild-harvested traditions; the concerns the industry itself reports centre on agave price cycles and the push for faster industrial cooking rather than species pressure.

traditions.name: Mezcal
traditions.origin: Deeply rooted in Oaxaca, with production across several states.
traditions.history: The denomination of origin permits any agave species; the category spans everything from cultivated espadín to rare wild agaves.
traditions.legalStatus: Spirit with its own Denomination of Origin; NOM-070-SCFI-2016 defines three production categories (mezcal, mezcal artesanal, mezcal ancestral) and six classes: blanco o joven, madurado en vidrio, reposado (2–12 months in wood), añejo (over 12 months in wood), abocado con and destilado con. Joven and abocado are different classes, not synonyms, and mezcal's requirements differ from tequila's even where minimums coincide. Tobalá is a wild agave under sustainability pressure, not a legal class of its own.
traditions.materials: Any agave species permitted by the denomination: cultivated espadín (Agave angustifolia), wild and cultivated tobalá (Agave potatorum), among many others.
traditions.practices: NOM-070 permits several equipment paths per category: pit, mampostería or autoclave cooking in the base category; pit or elevated mampostería ovens in artesanal; pit ovens in ancestral. Artisanal distillation may use copper alembics or clay pots (ollas de barro with clay/wood/copper monteras); ancestral uses clay pots with fuego directo. Pechuga is a destilado con practice, not a separate category. Not all mezcal is pit-roasted or smoky — the category-level process allows other cooking methods.
traditions.diversity: Batches vary a lot; an ensamble needs a known mix of agaves behind it; smoke depends on the cook, not the category.
traditions.sustainability: Mezcal spans cultivated espadín and many wild-harvested species; sustainability pressure concentrates on the wild-harvested end of the range (see the plant pages for species-level detail).

traditions.name: Bacanora
traditions.origin: A Sonoran distilling tradition from the Sierra (mountain country) of Sonora.
traditions.history: Long a regional practice; Sonoran official history describes a 1915–1992 prohibition era, with production legalized again in 1992. The denomination of origin was declared in 2000 — legalization and the DO are separate events, not one 2000 change.
traditions.legalStatus: Spirit with its own Denomination of Origin (Sonora, since 2000); official coverage is municipal within Sonora, not the whole state.
traditions.materials: Wild and cultivated Agave angustifolia, known locally as Pacifica or Yaquiana.
traditions.practices: Pit roast (often mesquite-fueled), wild-yeast fermentation, double distillation in vinatas.
traditions.diversity: Wild-harvested silvestre batches coexist with cultivated expressions; local plant names are preserved without settling the botany.
traditions.sustainability: Bacanora relies on wild yaquiana/Pacifica populations in the Sonoran Sierra; harvest pressure on wild agave is the tradition's main sustainability topic (category reporting reviewed 2026-10-21).

traditions.name: Raicilla
traditions.origin: A Jalisco tradition with two distinct styles, Sierra and Costa.
traditions.history: Historically a clandestine rural spirit in Jalisco's mountains; protected as a denomination of origin in 2019.
traditions.legalStatus: Spirit with its own Denomination of Origin (Jalisco and Bahía de Banderas, Nayarit, since 2019); the declaration names specific municipalities. Costa and Sierra are styles, not legal classes; reposado is a legally defined aged class under the DO.
traditions.materials: Several agaves: maximiliana (Sierra signature), angustifolia/chico aguiar, rhodacantha and others (Costa).
traditions.practices: Adobe-oven or pit roast, open wild-yeast fermentation in wooden vats, small-batch distillation; taberna is the local word for a small distillery.
traditions.diversity: Sierra and Costa bottlings differ in plant, roast and still; batches vary by taberna.
traditions.sustainability: Parts of the raicilla range depend on wild-harvested maximiliana and related species. Producers differ on sustainability, and only some have evidence to show for it.

traditions.name: Tuxca
traditions.origin: A regional tradition of the Jalisco–Colima borderlands around Tuxcacuesco.
traditions.history: A vinatero tradition predating modern categories; made in small batches from wild agaves.
traditions.legalStatus: A regional tradition with no denomination of origin; its legal status is not equivalent to tequila or mezcal, and absence of a NOM does not mean inauthentic.
traditions.materials: Wild agaves, often Liñeño/Cimarrón (Agave angustifolia and local relatives); ensambles vary by vinatero and batch.
traditions.practices: Cylindrical pit roast, hand-mash, volcanic crater fermentation, wooden Filipino still distillation.
traditions.diversity: Batches vary in what goes into them; the mix of agaves is only named when a source says what went into that batch.

traditions.name: Comiteco
traditions.origin: A sap-derived tradition from Comitán, Chiapas; protected as an Indicación Geográfica since October 2025.
traditions.history: Made from aguamiel collected from cultivated maguey comiteco (identified as Agave americana L. in the 2025 IG declaration; some other references and producer/importer material name Agave atrovirens — both names are kept here rather than quietly picking one); the piña is never cooked.
traditions.legalStatus: A regional tradition protected since 6 October 2025 as the Indicación Geográfica “Comiteco de Comitán, Chiapas” (an IG, not a denomination of origin like tequila or mezcal). The declaration covers a spirit made from maguey comiteco (Agave americana L.) and cane sugars in the Meseta Comiteca-Tojolabal; comiteco outside that scope is not automatically covered. Añejo remains a producer expression unless defined in the applicable IG rules — check each bottle.
traditions.materials: Aguamiel from the living maguey comiteco (Agave americana L. per the IG declaration; some sources name Agave atrovirens); the protected name explicitly includes cane sugars alongside agave, and composition stays a per-bottle fact — do not label any bottle 100% agave.
traditions.practices: Sap collection, fermentation, distillation in copper; blanco unaged, añejo rested in glass with white oak branches (no barrel maturation) per the example producer.
traditions.diversity: Composition disclosure varies by bottling, so it's listed bottle by bottle, not for the whole category.

traditions.name: Destilado de pulque
traditions.origin: A Tlaxcala and central-México tradition rooted in the pulque heartland.
traditions.history: Aguamiel is fermented into pulque (about 48 hours) and then distilled; the piña is never cooked.
traditions.legalStatus: A regional tradition; no denomination of origin, and explicitly not mezcal. Fermented pulque itself is not a spirit and is not catalogued.
traditions.materials: Aguamiel from cultivated maguey pulquero (Agave salmiana), collected daily from the living plant.
traditions.diversity: Small-producer batches; bottle-specific documentation is the rule.

traditions.name: Sotol
traditions.origin: A northern tradition of the Chihuahuan desert, centered in Chihuahua.
traditions.history: Made from Dasylirion (desert spoon), a related genus in the Asparagaceae family — explicitly not an agave, though agave-adjacent.
traditions.legalStatus: Spirit with its own Denomination of Origin (Chihuahua, Coahuila, Durango, since 2002); included here as an agave-adjacent northern tradition with its botanical distinction kept explicit.
traditions.materials: Wild-harvested Dasylirion (commonly wheeleri, cedrosanum or leiophyllum) after 8–12 years; a single plant yields roughly one bottle.
traditions.practices: Piña pit roast in conical ovens (or steam cooking by larger producers), wild fermentation, distillation in copper or clay; harvest practice and species determine whether roots are left intact — regrowth is not guaranteed by harvest alone.
traditions.diversity: Sustainability of harvest and conservation programs matter; the app never misclassifies Dasylirion as an agave.
